record.title: OpenVLHarness reports broad gains from visual evidence tools and persistent multimodal memory
record.summary: An Oct 19 arXiv preprint introduces OpenVLHarness, a training-free multimodal agent stack with nine task-level capabilities, outputs rendered as inspectable evidence, and per-query memory that keeps images, structured results and web references reusable across turns. Across 22 benchmarks and eight open/proprietary backbones, the authors report 9.7-12.6 point average gains over matched no-tool baselines. In their GPT-6 Luna comparison, medium-effort OpenVLHarness averages 56.5 versus 48.0 for the base model at maximum effort, 48.6 for Codex at maximum and 48.8 for Visual Sketchpad at maximum. These are author-reported benchmark results: Qwen3-VL results average three runs, while proprietary-model results are single runs; no independent reproduction was conducted. Model-token accounting excludes tool execution and judging, and the paper's abstract/prose cost summary conflicts with Table 2 for Codex.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that OpenVLHarness, a training-free multimodal agent harness combining task-level perception/search/computation tools, model-facing evidence rendering and per-query reusable multimodal artifacts, improved average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines across 22 benchmarks and eight open/proprietary backbones.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: On GPT-6 Luna, the authors report a 56.5 average at medium effort for OpenVLHarness versus 48.0 for the base model at maximum effort, 48.6 for Codex at maximum effort and 48.8 for Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort across their 22 benchmarks.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper and repository do not establish independent reproduction, generalization beyond the evaluated benchmarks/models, or lower end-to-end cost after tool execution, infrastructure and judging are included.

contradictory_evidence: Internal paper arithmetic discrepancy (arXiv HTML abstract and §3.3 versus Table 2): the prose says Luna medium uses at most 37% of compared methods' model-token cost at max. Displayed costs are $1.15/1k for Luna-medium OpenVLHarness and $2.52/1k for maximum-effort Codex, a 46% ratio; the other ratios are 36% of Base and 22% of Visual Sketchpad. This review uses the exact displayed table values and does not infer a reason for the mismatch.

evidence_gaps.description: The broad score improvements have not been independently reproduced; run-to-run uncertainty is reported for Qwen3-VL but not quantified for single-run proprietary model outcomes.
Token cost excludes external tool execution, GPU services, search API and judging, and the Luna cost summary conflicts with Table 2 for Codex.
Live web retrieval changes between runs, and results from proprietary backbones are single-run API evaluations.

brief.importance_rationale: If sustained across independent implementations and broader tasks, a multimodal tool-and-memory harness that improves scores across multiple open and proprietary backbones could materially change agent-system design and inference-budget allocation. The paper is one author-reported study with single-run proprietary evaluations and tool execution costs excluded, so the consequence is substantial but not yet generalizable.
limitations: All empirical results are from one author team and have not been independently reproduced in this review.
Only Qwen3-VL results use three independent runs; proprietary GPT-5, GPT-6 and Kimi results are single runs because of API cost.
Benchmarks cover selected visual perception, search, VQA and spatial tasks; they do not establish general agent capability or broad production performance.
Reported token costs omit tool execution, GPU services, external search and judging costs, so they are not end-to-end economic results.
The paper's abstract and §3.3 prose claim at most 37% of competitor token cost for Luna medium versus competitors at max, but Table 2 implies 46% of Codex max cost; cause is unresolved.
brief.summary: An Oct 19 arXiv preprint introduces OpenVLHarness, a training-free multimodal agent stack with nine task-level capabilities, outputs rendered as inspectable evidence, and per-query memory that keeps images, structured results and web references reusable across turns. Across 22 benchmarks and eight open/proprietary backbones, the authors report 9.7-12.6 point average gains over matched no-tool baselines. In their GPT-6 Luna comparison, medium-effort OpenVLHarness averages 56.5 versus 48.0 for the base model at maximum effort, 48.6 for Codex at maximum and 48.8 for Visual Sketchpad at maximum. These are author-reported benchmark results: Qwen3-VL results average three runs, while proprietary-model results are single runs; no independent reproduction was conducted. Model-token accounting excludes tool execution and judging, and the paper's abstract/prose cost summary conflicts with Table 2 for Codex.

technical.claimed_result: Across 22 benchmark datasets and eight backbones, the paper reports average improvements of 9.7-12.6 points over no-tool baselines. Qwen3-VL-8B rises from 34.2 to 45.4 and Qwen3-VL-32B from 38.3 to 50.9. On Luna, medium-effort OpenVLHarness scores 56.5 versus 48.0 for the base model, 48.6 for Codex and 48.8 for Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports model-token cost per 1,000 questions but excludes tool execution and judging. At Luna medium effort, Table 2 lists $1.15 versus maximum-effort costs $3.17 for Base, $2.52 for Codex and $5.15 for Visual Sketchpad; this is about 36%, 46% and 22%, respectively. The prose/abstract says the cost is at most 37% of the compared methods, which conflicts with the displayed Codex ratio. Tool services also require GPU-backed perception workers and a paid search API per the repository setup.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint and official code repository are accessible. The reported benchmark outcomes remain author-reported; no independent execution or reproduction was performed.
technical.mechanism: The capability layer defines task-level interfaces for five perception tools, three information-seeking tools and a coding agent; renderers turn heterogeneous results into readable observations. A per-query registry stores images, masks, arrays, structured outputs and web references under reusable handles, enabling later calls and code to inspect or combine the same evidence.
technical.regime: Training-free multimodal tool use on 22 selected benchmarks in grounded perception, visual search/deep research, general VQA/hallucination and spatial reasoning, using four open and four proprietary backbones. Qwen3-VL results average three seeds; proprietary GPT-5/GPT-6 and Kimi results are single runs.
technical.reproducibility: The authors release the implementation, evaluation loaders, presets and instructions. The repository lists seven of eight paper presets and states exact reproduction requires specific model-serving versions/configurations and a second Qwen3-VL-8B service for the auxiliary search role. It warns that a small sampled installation check does not reproduce the paper scores. Independent reproduction and all-in cost measurement remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: Matched no-tool baseline and training-free harnesses Visual Sketchpad, Codex and OctoTools on shared Qwen3-VL settings; a separate Luna comparison evaluates five effort settings and 22,000+ questions per setting.

brief.title: OpenVLHarness reports broad gains from visual evidence tools and persistent multimodal memory
brief.why_it_matters: If the results generalize, a training-free evidence-and-memory harness can improve multimodal task performance more than increasing model reasoning effort alone in the tested regimes, changing how agent teams allocate inference compute and tool engineering. The result is bounded by selected benchmarks/models, first-party evaluation, single-run proprietary scores and incomplete end-to-end cost accounting.
